answers.question: What was the task?
answers.answer: The task was to rename the server timeout setting so that its name shows milliseconds.
quotes: The task was to rename the server timeout setting so that its name shows milliseconds.

answers.question: How did it end: what is done and what is not?
answers.answer: The rename is done in the code and in the settings file, and both tests pass; the operations team's production file still sets the timeout under the old name and was left alone.
quotes: That is done in the code and in our settings file, and both tests pass.
The operations team's production file still sets the timeout under the old name.
I left that file alone, because changes to it go through operations.

answers.question: How does the thing that changed work?
answers.answer: The code now reads only the new name and falls back to five seconds when the name is missing; production loads the settings file and puts the operations file on top of it.
quotes: The code now reads only the new name.
When the name is missing, it falls back to five seconds.
Production loads our settings file and puts the operations file on top of it.

answers.question: What is the problem, and what causes it?
answers.answer: After the release production waits three seconds instead of ten, because the operations file still sets the timeout under the old name, which the code no longer reads.
quotes: The code no longer reads that name, so after the release production waits three seconds instead of ten.
The operations file sets ten seconds under the old name.

answers.question: What is not verified?
answers.answer: The loading of the production file is not verified: the author knows it from a comment in the code and did not see the loading itself, and the tests do not read the production file.
quotes: I know this from a comment in the code; I did not see the loading itself.
They do not read the production file.
